The father is the one being held captive. The kidnapper has forced the daughter to speak over a smartphone; she begs for her father's life to be spared, while the kidnapper shouts the demand: bring one hundred million yen alone by noon tomorrow, or the hostage (her father) dies, with no police. Hearing this, the father decides that the ransom should not be paid. His reason is the "alone" condition and his love for his daughter: if she obeyed, she would have to bring the money by herself into the hands of dangerous criminals. He fears she would be harmed, taken hostage herself, or subjected to further extortion. Rather than let his daughter walk alone into that danger to save him, he chooses to refuse the ransom—accepting his own fate to keep her out of harm's way.

Does the father refuse to be ransomed because he knows the daughter cannot possibly raise one hundred million yen—so the demand is impossible for her, and he doesn't want her to be driven to desperate or dangerous measures trying?
Does the father's refusal hinge on the deadline "by noon tomorrow"—for example, that paying wouldn't happen in time, or that the tight deadline is meant to force the daughter into reckless action?

Is the key that the kidnapper said "no police," and the father, hearing this and knowing the daughter would have to come alone, decides the ransom should not be paid because that is the safest way to allow the police to be involved and rescue him?
Does the father believe that the daughter's plea is not freely made but coerced by the kidnapper—so that if ransom is not paid, the kidnapper has less reason to keep her involved or at risk?

The father is able to communicate, and he instructs her not to pay. His reason is the demand's "alone" condition and his love for his daughter: he understands that obeying would send her, by herself, into the hands of dangerous criminals. She might be harmed, taken hostage too, or extorted further. Rather than let her risk herself to save him—even though she is begging to spare his life—he chooses to refuse the ransom, overruling her plea and accepting his own fate so that she stays out of danger.

The father is the hostage. Over a smartphone, the kidnapper makes the daughter beg for her father's life to be spared and shouts the demand: one hundred million yen, brought alone by noon tomorrow, no police, or the hostage dies. The father, able to communicate, tells her not to pay.

His reason is the trap hidden in the demand. The insistence that the money be brought alone, by the daughter, with no police, is not a genuine exchange for his life—it is a setup to lure her by herself into the kidnapper's hands, where she would be seized or harmed. He realizes that if she obeys, she will not save him but will walk into the same danger, and that the kidnapper is someone who would harm her too. So he overrules her plea and refuses the ransom, preferring to risk his own life rather than let his daughter be lured alone into a trap.

Is the essential reason the father refuses that the kidnapper intends to kill the father regardless—so that the only real effect of the daughter delivering the money would be to put her in the killer's power?
Does the father refuse because he has already made peace with dying—for example, he is old or terminally ill—so the money would be better used by the daughter, and her risk would be pointless?
Is the father's refusal because the daughter is not capable of delivering the ransom safely without police involvement—she would have to go alone, which he considers unacceptable?

Does the father refuse because he recognizes the "kidnapper" as someone who cannot actually carry out the threat—for example, a child, or a person in custody, or someone the father knows is bluffing?

Is the father's refusal because he is not the daughter's real father—for example, he is a stranger who received her call by mistake, or a police negotiator posing as her father—so the money is not his to decide and he declines?

The father is the hostage. Over a smartphone, the kidnapper makes the daughter speak: she begs for her father's life to be spared, while the kidnapper shouts the demand—one hundred million yen, brought alone by noon tomorrow, no police, or the hostage dies. The father, who can communicate, tells her not to pay.

His reason is the demand's "alone" condition and his fear for her. The instruction that she bring the money by herself, without police, makes her unprotected and vulnerable. If she obeys, she would walk into the kidnapper's hands, where she could be seized, harmed, or extorted further; the kidnapper is someone who would harm her too. The father recognizes that paying would not reliably save him and would instead put his daughter in danger. So, even though she is begging to spare his life, he overrules her plea and refuses the ransom—accepting his own fate rather than letting her risk herself alone for him.
